newsitem.title: UK: MG looking into Shanghai metals prospects.
newsitem.headline: MG looking into Shanghai metals prospects.

text.p: Germany's Metallgesellschaft AG is looking into opportunities in the physical metals sector in Shanghai, an official of its London-based metals subsidiary said on Monday.
Christian Schirmeister, Associate Director for Client Liaison at MG unit Metallgesellschaft Ltd, said the company had recently changed its structure for the Far East.
Two of its London staff had gone out to Shanghai a month ago, complementing the 12 employees already at its Hong Kong operation and its liaison office in Beijing.
"We're now studying the business opportunities in Shanghai," Schirmeister told Reuters in an interview.

Metallgesellschaft currently did what he called a "fair amount" of metals business with China, although obtaining exact information on the market situation there and dealing with a mixture of state-run and free-market operators could be difficult.
"So far all contracts have been met, some faster than others, but we haven't had any problem," he said. "It's a process of learning for both sides."

The scale of China's internal production, its strategic stocks and the volumes needed for the Shanghai Metal Exchange were roughly known, but Metallgesellschaft had to watch movements of metal in and out of the country and also monitor the regional scrap markets.

China's copper deficit could be between 100,000 and 300,000 tonnes, but it was waiting to see how the market developed before moving in to buy. Besides, there was only a limited period when Chinese buyers could use foreign exchange funds to import metals.
London-based traders say China traditionally comes into the market in the second half of the year.

Schirmeister said Metallgesellschaft Ltd, a ring-dealing member of the London Metal Exchange (LME), had taken on a few staff members from the Shearson Lehman team in London and abroad since Lehman Brothers Commodities pulled out of the LME floor last November.
The departure of Lehman Brothers and of Deutsche Sharps Pixley some six months later had reduced the number of ring-trading companies to 15 and increased risk on the market, Schirmeister said.

"Less players, you have to take more risk. You have to spread the same cake around fewer people, which is making life difficult sometimes. What we need is a liquid market with strong professional participants and obviously the more the better," he said.

However, Metallgesellschaft Ltd was on its way to achieving its $40-million profit target for the year ended September 30, 1997. That would be roughly twice the level of its earnings in 1995-96, when copper prices fell sharply in the wake of the Sumitomo scandal.
